title: Forms of bound labour in the ancient world
content: Slavery in the ancient world is often imagined on the model of plantation systems that arose much later, with a sharp line drawn between free persons and property. The evidence from ancient civilizations describes something far more varied and considerably harder to summarize. Legal status ran along a spectrum that included debt bondage for a fixed term, service owed to a temple, hereditary obligation attached to a plot of land, and outright ownership of a person who could be sold at will. Individuals moved between these conditions across a lifetime, and a single ancient household might contain several of them at once. What the categories shared was compulsion, yet the compulsion took different forms and carried very different prospects. A debt bondsman expected release at the end of his term, and his children were usually born free; a captive taken in an ancient war might be sold abroad and never return to the region of his birth. In some ancient cities enslaved people held property, conducted business, and purchased their own freedom, while in the mines of that same society others died within a few years of arriving. The single word that covers all of this conceals more than it reveals to us. Historians accordingly attend to what a given arrangement demanded and what it permitted rather than to the label attached to it. This approach makes comparison across ancient civilizations possible without assuming that a common term names a common institution, and it prevents the modern image from being read backward into periods where the arrangements it describes had not yet appeared.
